name: Sheerness
title: Sheerness Thickness Gauging | Car Carriers, Reefers, Ro-Ro
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement at Sheerness on the Medway for car carriers, reefer, ro-ro and forest products ships: decks, ramps, holds and tanks.
h1: Ship Thickness Measurement at the Port of Sheerness and the Medway
intro: Sheerness, on the Isle of Sheppey at the mouth of the Medway, is one of Britain's busiest vehicle import ports and a major landing point for fresh fruit and forest products. Its berths are tidal but free of locks, so car carriers, refrigerated cargo ships, ro-ro freighters and pulp and paper carriers arrive and sail on schedule. Gauging is planned into those calls. The technicians are mobilised from India for each job and board at the berth with access arranged by the ship's agent.

highlights.p: Car carriers discharging at Sheerness leave their decks empty for a short spell. Deck plating, hoistable deck supports and internal ramps can be gauged and checked for cracks in that gap, before the next deck is loaded or the ship sails on her rotation.

highlights.h: Fruit services on a fixed pattern
highlights.p: Fresh produce arrives on refrigerated services that call week after week. Cargo spaces stay closed and cold, so the scope concentrates on deck structure, hatch covers and the sea-water piping that cools the refrigeration plant, planned against a schedule known well ahead.

Pulp, paper and timber ships discharge steadily over a day or more. Tank tops, hold frames and hatch covers can be gauged as each hold is cleared, which makes these ships the longest and most predictable gauging windows at the port.

p: Sheerness stands at the north-western corner of the Isle of Sheppey, where the Medway meets the Thames Estuary, and the port occupies the site of the former Royal Navy dockyard. Ships approach from the estuary's main channels into the Medway, with the Isle of Grain on the opposite shore, and berth directly on the tidal river with no lock or air-draught restriction to plan around. Medway Ports, part of Peel Ports, is the harbour authority and runs the port. Off Sheerness lies the wreck of the SS Richard Montgomery, a Second World War munitions ship, inside a marked exclusion zone that every ship keeps clear of on the approach, and the estuary's shallows mean channels and tides still decide the timing of deep-laden arrivals.

Vehicles are the port's best-known trade. Hundreds of thousands of new cars, vans and trucks pass through each year, with large secure storage areas behind the quays, and deep-sea and short-sea car carriers call on regular rotations. Fresh produce is the second pillar: a dedicated fruit terminal with temperature-controlled storage and banana ripening rooms handles regular refrigerated services. Forest products, chiefly pulp and paper for the mills of Kent, together with timber, steel, project cargo and ro-ro freight make up the rest, and a short-sea ro-ro service carrying unaccompanied trailers has linked the port with Calais. Across the river mouth, the Isle of Grain has an LNG import terminal and a container terminal, which bring LNG carriers and container ships into the same approaches.

Each trade has its own rhythm. Car carriers work quickly, discharging and loading deck by deck, and their stay is measured in hours to a day. Fruit services run to a weekly pattern that seldom changes, so a ship's next Sheerness call is known well in advance. Forest products ships stay longer, discharging bales and rolls over a day or more, and are often older short-sea tonnage. Winter brings northerly and easterly gales across the Thames Estuary, which can delay arrivals and stop launch work but affects the berths far less. For gauging, the predictable schedules make it straightforward to plan a scope across two or three consecutive calls with the same reference points.

facilities.h: Gauging berths and windows at Sheerness
p: Sheerness is a cargo port rather than a repair port, so gauging here is done afloat during cargo calls. At the vehicle berths the team works on decks the stevedores have cleared, with the ship's crew providing lighting and safe access to hoistable decks, and moves deck by deck behind the discharge. On ro-ro freighters the stern ramp, its hinges and the main vehicle deck take the hardest wear, and they are best inspected in the gap between unloading and loading. On refrigerated cargo ships, deck and machinery-space work fits around the cargo, because the cargo spaces must stay closed and cold until they are worked.

Forest products berths give the longest working time. Holds empty over the course of the discharge, and tank tops, frames and hatch covers can be gauged as each hold is cleared. Ships waiting in the estuary for a berth or a tide sometimes anchor off the Medway, and launch-borne deck work can be arranged through the agent in fair weather, although the estuary's short, steep sea in a northerly blow ends that option quickly. For docking, ships on these trades generally go to yards on the near Continent or elsewhere in Britain, and the readings from a Sheerness call travel with the specification.
list: Vehicle berths: car deck plating, hoistable deck supports and internal ramp gauging, with crack detection, on car carriers between discharge and loading.
Ro-ro berths: stern ramp, hinge and main vehicle deck structure on trailer ferries during the turnaround.
Fresh fruit terminal: deck structure, hatch covers and sea-water cooling piping on refrigerated cargo ships, worked around cargo operations.
Forest products and steel berths: hold-by-hold tank-top, frame and hatch cover gauging during discharge.
Thames Estuary anchorages: short launch-borne deck and air-pipe scopes on ships waiting for a berth, weather permitting.

context.h: Port state control, vehicle-carrier scrutiny and the car trade
p: The Maritime and Coastguard Agency carries out port state control at Sheerness, and the UK continues to apply the Paris MoU through national regulations. Vehicle carriers have drawn particular scrutiny in recent years after serious fires that started in cargo on car decks, and inspectors, insurers and charterers now look closely at the condition of decks, ramps, fire boundaries and fixed fire-fighting pipework. Wasted ramp structure or a corroded fire main on a car carrier is a finding that all of them take seriously, and current thickness and crack-detection records are the most direct answer to it.

The car trade has its own commercial pattern. Many car carriers are chartered by vehicle logistics companies on long contracts, and a large number of new ships have joined the trade since the early 2020s, often with dual-fuel engines, while older ships run on beside them. On the older ships, decks and ramps have carried countless vehicle movements, and owners need to know where deck plating and stiffeners are thinning before an intermediate or renewal survey, or before a charter ends. Fruit trades rely on refrigeration plant whose sea-water cooling lines corrode steadily and are simple to check while the ship works cargo.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs at Sheerness
jobs.p: Sheerness jobs follow the cargo. Car carrier and ro-ro work concentrates on decks, ramps and the structure that supports them, combining ultrasonic thickness readings with magnetic particle testing where cracks are suspected. Forest products and steel ships get hold and hatch cover gauging during discharge, much as they would at any bulk berth. Refrigerated cargo ships are usually scoped for machinery-space piping and deck structure. Because these trades run on fixed rotations, we often agree a scope that spans two or three calls, with the same reference points each time, so the work never holds up a sailing.
list: Car deck plating and hoistable deck support gauging on a car carrier approaching her intermediate survey, with MPI at lifting-point welds.
Stern ramp hinge and ramp structure inspection on a ro-ro freighter after reported cracking, done during the turnaround.
Sea-water cooling and fire-main pipe gauging on a refrigerated cargo ship, mapped to the piping drawings so spools can be ordered.
Tank-top and hold frame gauging on a forest products ship discharging pulp and paper, hold by hold.
Off-hire condition gauging of a chartered car carrier before redelivery, giving owner and charterer a shared record of deck and ramp condition.

logistics: Teams usually fly into London Heathrow, Gatwick or London City and travel to the Isle of Sheppey by road, or by rail with a change at Sittingbourne for the branch line to Sheerness-on-Sea. The technicians travel from India and need UK visas, which take longer to arrange than a car carrier's rotation, so we work from the published schedule and book the call we will meet well ahead. Port access is controlled; the ship's agent requests passes from the port against each technician's passport and confirms the berth.

faqs.q: Can car decks be gauged during a Sheerness discharge?
faqs.a: Yes, deck by deck. As the stevedores clear each deck, the team gauges deck plating and stiffeners and checks hoistable deck supports and ramp structure, with the crew providing lighting and safe access to raised decks. We agree the order with the chief officer so that we are never on a deck that is about to be loaded or moved. Larger scopes are spread over consecutive calls.

faqs.q: Do you inspect ro-ro ramps for cracks as well as thickness?
faqs.a: Yes. Stern ramps, ramp hinges and the deck structure around them carry repeated wheel loads and impact, so cracking at welded connections matters as much as wastage. We combine ultrasonic thickness readings with magnetic particle testing at the welds, and report findings against the ship's frame numbering so the superintendent can plan repairs with the yard or the next riding crew.

faqs.q: Is the Port of Sheerness affected by locks or tides?
faqs.a: There is no lock: the berths sit directly on the tidal Medway, and ships come straight alongside from the estuary. The tide still changes gangway angles and the height of the ship against the quay through the day, so we plan access to upper decks and external structure with that in mind, and confirm boarding times with the agent once the berth is fixed.

faqs.q: Can you gauge ships at anchor off Sheerness?
faqs.a: Occasionally. Ships waiting for a Medway berth or the tide may anchor in the Thames Estuary, and a short deck and air-pipe scope can be done by launch arranged through the agent. The estuary is shallow and exposed to the north and east, so a short, steep sea can stop launch work quickly. Where there is a choice, we board once the ship is alongside.
